questions.q: Why does this lesson say a DR runbook that has never actually been executed is a guess rather than a working plan?
options: Because runbooks are always written in the wrong file format
Because runbooks are only required for active-active architectures
Because a document describes what should happen but says nothing about whether it actually happens — only running it proves that
Because a runbook automatically updates itself once infrastructure drifts
questions.explain: A runbook describes intended behavior. Infrastructure drift, stale credentials, hardcoded references, and departed staff all mean the document can diverge from reality in ways rereading it will never reveal — only execution does.

questions.q: What is a tabletop exercise, and what is its real limitation according to this lesson?
options: It is walking through a runbook as a group without executing it; it catches obvious gaps like missing owners but cannot catch execution-time failures such as a stale DNS TTL or a hardcoded database endpoint
It is a full production failover, and it has no real limitations
It is a chaos-engineering game day, and it always finds every execution-time failure
It is a type of backup job, unrelated to failover planning
questions.explain: A tabletop exercise narrates the runbook without running it, which is useful for surfacing ambiguous steps but cannot catch failures that only appear in execution, like a DNS record's TTL or an IAM role missing a permission.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the only way to actually measure whether a DR design meets its RTO and RPO targets, rather than estimate them?
options: Reading the architecture diagram carefully one more time
Asking the cloud provider's support team to confirm the numbers
Calculating the numbers from the published specifications of each service involved
Running a real failover drill and watching how long recovery and data loss actually take
questions.explain: You can estimate that a warm standby should take over within some number of minutes, but the only way to know the real number is to start a clock during an actual drill and watch DNS propagate, the secondary promote, and the application come back.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that a failed DR test is more valuable than a DR plan that has simply never been tested?
options: A failed test surfaces a real gap — like an expired credential or missing permission — before a real disaster finds it instead, under uncontrolled conditions
A failed test automatically fixes the underlying configuration problem
Failed tests are required by regulation in every industry
An untested plan is always safer than a tested one
questions.explain: An untested plan carries the same hidden risk as a failed test — the gap is just undiscovered. A failed test finds that gap on a controlled schedule, which is strictly better than finding it during a real, uncontrolled disaster.

questions.q: Which of the following is given in this lesson as an example of a specific execution-time failure that only a real drill, not a tabletop exercise, would reveal?
options: A missing step owner that's obvious just from reading the runbook aloud
A DNS record with a longer TTL than anyone remembered, causing traffic to keep hitting the dead region far longer than the runbook assumes
An ambiguous escalation path that a group discussion easily identifies
A step nobody present can explain the reason for
questions.explain: A stale DNS TTL is invisible on paper and only becomes apparent when someone actually executes a failover and watches traffic continue hitting the dead region longer than expected — exactly the kind of gap a tabletop exercise cannot surface.
